citation: Maffezzoli, M., Monaca, F., Cantale, O., Gomez-Randulfe, I., Teoh, A., Htun, L., ..., & Banna, G. L. (2026). TTF-1 and PD-L1 interplay as prognostic biomarkers in first-line metastatic lung adenocarcinoma: a multicentre real-world study. The oncologist, oyag469.
title: TTF-1 and PD-L1 interplay as prognostic biomarkers in first-line metastatic lung adenocarcinoma: a multicentre real-world study
abstract: Introduction Thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1) is routinely assessed in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) as a diagnostic marker. Evidence suggests that TTF-1 may also have prognostic relevance in metastatic NSCLC (aNSCLC). We investigated the prognostic impact of TTF-1 expression in aNSCLC receiving first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based therapy and its interplay with PD-L1. Methods This was a multicentre retrospective real-world study including patients with aNSCLC treated at five UK institutions with first-line ICI monotherapy or chemoimmunotherapy (CT+ICI) between 2017 and 2025. Outcomes were analysed according to TTF-1 status and PD-L1 expression, primarily in patients with adenocarcinoma (ADK). Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) was included as an exploratory comparator. Results Among 823 patients, 288 (35.0%) were TTF-1 negative (TTF1-) and 535 (65.0%) TTF-1 positive (TTF1+). TTF1- tumours included ADK (121, 42.0%) and SCC (167, 58.0%). TTF1-/ADK had shorter PFS (5.79 vs 9.90 months, HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.25-1.93, p Conclusions TTF1-/ADK showed worse outcomes, with the strongest prognostic association in the PD-L1 1-49% subgroup. These findings support further investigation of prognostic heterogeneity and require independent validation.

citation: Elzein, A., Sideris, N., Dixon, A. C., Galvácsi, A., Bodnár, N., Kállay, C., ..., & Kostakis, G. E. (2026). Salpyran ligands at the interface of copper chemistry and biology: structure-function relationships, metal selectivity, redox control, and biological interactions. Dalton transactions (Cambridge, England : 2003), 55(45), 16154-16171.
title: Salpyran ligands at the interface of copper chemistry and biology: structure-function relationships, metal selectivity, redox control, and biological interactions
abstract: This study evaluates Salpyran, a tetradentate N 3 O ligand, and electronically modified derivatives. Systematic potentiometry reveals that substituent effects modestly modulate metal binding without significantly improving Cu(II)/Zn(II) selectivity. Direct comparison with trientine identifies an unexpected Fe(III) preference for Salpyran, thus limiting its application as a copper-selective chelator but provides key design principles for future structural refinement. Our data shows that. Cu(II)-Salpyran suppresses ROS generation, protects peptides from oxidation, and binds DNA non-oxidatively. Proof-of-concept 64 Cu radiolabelling shows PET imaging compatibility, though Fe(III) competition requires framework refinement. Cytotoxicity studies reveal context-dependent antiproliferative activity: copper coordination enhances potency in most cancer lines but reduces it in carboplatin-resistant NSCLC models, without cross-resistance. This work establishes Salpyran as a versatile platform and provides design principles linking ligand structure, metal selectivity, redox behaviour, and biological activity.

citation: Maffezzoli, M., Lau, J., Dungey, M., Postaleniec, E., Neola, G., Formisano, L., ..., & Banna, G. L. (2026). Survival Outcomes of Sequential Therapies in Malignant Pleural Mesothelioma: A Real-World Analysis of Second-Line Treatment With Nivolumab or Carboplatin-Pemetrexed. JCO oncology practice, OP2600765.
title: Survival Outcomes of Sequential Therapies in Malignant Pleural Mesothelioma: A Real-World Analysis of Second-Line Treatment With Nivolumab or Carboplatin-Pemetrexed
abstract: Purpose Optimal treatment sequencing in malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) remains uncertain, particularly after progression on first-line (1L) treatment. We assessed real-world outcomes of patients receiving second-line (2L) carboplatin-pemetrexed (CARBO-PEM) after nivolumab-ipilimumab (NIVO-IPI), or 2L nivolumab (NIVO) after CARBO-PEM and explored the prognostic value of the Mesothelioma Risk Score (MRS) in the 1L setting. Materials and methods This multicenter retrospective study included patients with advanced MPM treated across five UK institutions between May 2015 and November 2025. Eligible patients received either 2L CARBO-PEM after NIVO-IPI, or 1L CARBO-PEM followed by 2L NIVO. The primary end point was overall survival (OS) from 1L treatment initiation. Results Overall, 147 patients were included, and 54 received NIVO-IPI followed by CARBO-PEM and 93 received CARBO-PEM followed by NIVO. The median age was 73.8 years and 83.0% had epithelioid histology. The median follow-up was 43.3 months from 1L initiation. The median OS was 23.55 months with CARBO-PEM followed by NIVO versus 25.53 months with NIVO-IPI followed by CARBO-PEM (hazard ratio 1.28 [95% CI, 0.82 to 2.01]; P = .270). The median PFS 2L was 3.65 months with 2L NIVO versus 6.15 months with 2L CARBO-PEM, without statistical significance, while median OS 2L was 12.53 months and 14.11, respectively. In the 1L setting, MRS showed limited discrimination for PFS and OS. Grade ≥2 irAEs during NIVO-IPI were associated with longer PFS 1L but not OS. Conclusion In patients with MPM receiving 2L therapy, CARBO-PEM after NIVO-IPI remains clinically active, and OS appeared similar across treatment sequences. These findings support sequence flexibility in fit patients but highlight the need for more robust prognostic biomarkers.

citation: Carr, A. S., Bose, S., Clark, S., Cooksley, T., Fudge, T., Furlepa, M., ..., & Young, K. (2026). Cross-specialty Triple M syndrome clinical practice guide: immune checkpoint inhibitor associated myasthenia-myositis-myocarditis overlap syndrome. BMJ oncology, 5(2), e001365.
title: Cross-specialty Triple M syndrome clinical practice guide: immune checkpoint inhibitor associated myasthenia-myositis-myocarditis overlap syndrome
abstract: This guide is intended to assist clinicians in the diagnosis and management of Triple M syndrome (immune-checkpoint inhibitor associated myositis-myasthenia-myocarditis overlap syndrome). It is designed for cross-specialty use by oncologists, neurologists, cardiologists, intensivists, general practitioners and acute physicians as well as Allied Health Professionals in appropriate areas. This guide has been developed through a modified Delphi method to derive a multi-specialty consensus from clinical experts in acute oncology (AO-B, KY, HS, PN), neurology (ASC, SJ, JL, SB) and cardio-oncology (AKG, SDR). Input from relevant stakeholders including Intensive Care (SC, TF), general practice (SR), acute medicine (TC) as well as trainees in neurology (MF) and oncology (IW) was incorporated to improve deliverability and applicability. A systematic review of the immune checkpoint inhibitor literature reporting clinical features, management strategies and outcomes in Triple M syndrome. Diagnostic criteria and treatment escalation are based on case series and case reports identified through this search and specialty-specific experience. Advice regarding ICU and palliative care considerations is also provided. No prospective studies or clinical trials have been conducted in the treatment of Triple M syndrome. Hence, guidance is based on expert opinion utilising international best practice publications on management of immune-related toxicities of checkpoint inhibitor therapy in general (European Society for Medical Oncology and European Society of Cardiology). The clinical practice guide was reviewed by the Association of British Neurologists (ABN)-affiliated neuromuscular (including ASC, JL, SJ) and neuro-oncology (including SB) advisory groups and ABN quality committee, the respective boards of the British Cardio-Oncology Society (AKG/SDR), New and Emerging Oncotherapeutic Neurotoxicity Network, Immuno-oncology Clinical Network, UK Acute Oncology Society and the Society of Acute Medics to ensure quality and national applicability and to identify regional barriers to implementation. These guidelines will be reviewed in response to meaningful changes in clinical practice annually by the authors to consider newly published evidence under the governance of the ABN quality committee.

citation: White, N., Leaston, L., Taubert, M., Nwosu, A. C., Combes, S., Seal, M., ..., & Minton, O. (2026). Virtual Reality for Pain Management in Advanced Cancer: A Multi-Site Single-Arm Pre-post Study in Hospice and Hospital Settings. The American journal of hospice & palliative care, 10499091261508437.
title: Virtual Reality for Pain Management in Advanced Cancer: A Multi-Site Single-Arm Pre-post Study in Hospice and Hospital Settings
journal: The American journal of hospice & palliative care
abstract: ObjectivesPrimary: explore whether a single session of virtual reality (VR) was associated with reduced self-reported pain in people with advanced cancer. Secondary: describe baseline quality of life, symptom burden and pain interference; compare change in pain between hospice and hospital settings and describe acceptability and safety.MethodsSingle-arm pre-post study at four UK sites (two hospices, two hospitals). Adults with advanced cancer and pain in the past week were eligible. Participants completed the Brief Pain Inventory, EQ-5D-5 L, and EORTC QLQ-C30 before VR. They rated current pain (0-10) immediately before and after the session. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test assessed change.ResultsThirty-seven participants were recruited (hospice n = 19, hospital n = 18; median age 60; 65% female). Baseline symptom burden was high: QLQ-C30 fatigue and pain scores approached the scale maximum, and mean EQ-5D index was 0.34. Pain reduced from a median of 4 to 2 (z = 3.67, P P = 0.003) and hospital ( P = 0.024) settings, with no evidence of a difference between them ( P = 0.452). No serious adverse events occurred.ConclusionsA single VR session was well tolerated and associated with reduced self-reported pain, with early signals of similar effects across care settings. VR may offer a low-risk, non-pharmacological adjunct within multimodal pain management. Controlled trials are needed to establish efficacy, duration of effect and which patients benefit most.

citation: Harder, H., Hunter, R., Collinson, B., Jones, J., Street, T., Evans, C., Cowley, A., & Jenkins, V. (2026). Understanding multiple myeloma: insights into patients' experiences and preferences for communication, information and support. Hematology (Amsterdam, Netherlands), 31(1), 2762576.
title: Understanding multiple myeloma: insights into patients' experiences and preferences for communication, information and support
abstract: Objectives To explore the unmet communication, information, and support needs of people living with multiple myeloma (MM) and identify helpful and unhelpful phrases or behaviors used by family and friends (F&F) and healthcare professionals (HCPs) in the Patient Understanding of Multiple Myeloma and Communication Experiences (PUMMaCE) study. Methods An online survey was co-developed with HCPs and people living with MM, as part of the study. The survey consisted of closed- and open-ended questions. A framework analysis was conducted on the qualitative free-text responses to identify key themes related to patients' communication experiences and preferences. Results In total, 138 people living with MM completed the survey. The free-text comments were organized into six overarching themes. Making sense of MM, gaps in understanding MM, communicating MM to F&F, F&F behaviors, HCP interactions, and healthcare systems and pathways. Many felt confused by the complex terminology and had unanswered questions about their disease, treatment, and prognosis. Limited understanding often led to F&F exhibiting unhelpful behaviors. Yet, there were also examples of positive communication and behaviors that supported respondents in managing their day-to-day life. Discussion and conclusion Significant gaps in communication, information, and support exist in MM care. The findings of this survey illustrate the challenges posed by the complexity of the language used routinely by HCPs, which can lead to distress and misunderstandings. These data will be used to inform the production of educational materials to improve communication among patients, their families, and HCPs.

citation: Ibraheim, H., Davide d'Arienzo, P., James Dean, N., Singh, A., Bohar, B., Manickavasagar, T., ..., & Powell, N. (2026). A pragmatic endoscopic/histological classification of immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced colitis: clinical and transcriptomic correlates. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association, S1542-3565(26)00834-7.
title: A pragmatic endoscopic/histological classification of immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced colitis: clinical and transcriptomic correlates
journal: Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association
abstract: Background & aims Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) improve cancer outcomes but frequently induce ICI-colitis, causing significant morbidity, prolonged immunosuppression, and premature ICI discontinuation. Risk stratification using CTCAE diarrhoea grading is imprecise, highlighting the need for clinically and biologically informed classification. Methods Retrospective data from 250 patients at two U.K. centres were analysed. Endoscopic severity was graded by Mayo endoscopic score (MES). Associations were assessed using chi-squared and multivariable analysis. Transcriptomic profiling of colonic biopsies (18 patients, 18 controls) was performed for gene- and pathway-level analyses. Results Patients were classified into two endoscopic-histological phenotypes: Group 1, mild inflammation (MES 0-1), comprising Group 1a, non-microscopic colitis (69.4%) and Group 1b, microscopic colitis (10.5%); and Group 2, moderate-to-severe colitis (MES 2-3; 20%). Bloody stool, anti-CTLA-4 therapy, and anti-PD-(L)1 plus chemotherapy independently predicted Group 2 (AUC 0.79), which was associated with higher faecal calprotectin, hospitalisation, steroid-refractory disease, and surgery. Group 1b, associated with anti-PD-1(L1) therapy had the mildest phenotype with no bloody stool or grade 4 diarrhoea and fewer hospitalisations. Oral second-generation corticosteroids achieved >80% remission in Group 1. ICI re-challenge led to recurrence in ∼37%, typically of similar or lower severity. Transcriptomic profiling identified a shared inflammatory programme across groups, with Group 2 additionally enriched for VEGF signalling, extracellular matrix remodelling, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Conclusions Phenotype-driven classification of ICI-colitis captures clinically and biologically meaningful heterogeneity, identifies high-risk patients and informs therapeutic strategies. This framework supports earlier intervention in severe disease while enabling steroid-sparing approaches in lower-risk groups, reducing treatment-related morbidity.

citation: Alabas, O. A., Mason, K. J., Lunt, M., Ryan, S., Reynolds, N. J., Smith, C. H., Bunker, C. B., Griffiths, C. E. M., Green, A. C., & Warren, R. B. (2026). Risk of cancer in psoriasis patients treated with biologic therapy: A BADBIR cohort study. Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV.
title: Risk of cancer in psoriasis patients treated with biologic therapy: A BADBIR cohort study
journal: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
abstract: Background There are concerns that biologic therapies for psoriasis may increase cancer risk. Objectives To compare risks of (i) incident cancer excluding keratinocyte carcinomas (KC; hereafter referred to as cancer) and (ii) KC among patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis treated with biologic versus non-biologic systemic therapies, and across biologic classes. Methods Data from the British Association of Dermatologists Biologics and Immunomodulators Register (BADBIR), a UK and Republic of Ireland register collected 2007-2025, were linked to NHS Digital for enhanced cancer ascertainment. Biologic-naïve patients aged ≥16 years with chronic plaque psoriasis and no prior cancer or KC were included. Cancer or KC events occurring within 12 months of treatment initiation were excluded. Crude incidence rates per 1000 person-years (py) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. Adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs; 95% CI) were estimated using propensity score-weighted flexible parametric survival models with multiple imputation for missing data. Results The cancer and KC analyses included 18,894 and 19,144 patients, respectively (58% receiving biologics in both), reflecting differences in outcome-specific exclusion criteria. In 1-year lagged analyses, cancer incidence rates per 1000 person-years were 6.40 [95% CI 5.83-7.02] in biologic initiators and 6.83 [95% CI 6.01-7.76] in non-biologic systemic initiators, with an aHR of 0.91 [95% CI 0.77-1.07]. Corresponding KC incidence rates were 2.63 [95% CI 2.28-3.04] and 2.42 [95% CI 1.96-3.00], respectively, with an aHR of 1.05 [95% CI 0.81-1.35]. Follow-up was shorter for IL-12/23i and IL-17i than for TNFi. Cancer risk did not differ significantly for IL-12/23i or IL-17i versus TNFi, nor was KC risk elevated for IL-12/23i. Conclusions This real-world study found no evidence of an increased risk of cancer or KC with biologic compared with non-biologic systemic therapies, or across the biologic classes. Larger studies with longer follow-up, particularly for newer biologics, are needed to clarify long-term risk.

citation: Tsili, A. C., Pasoglou, V., Campo, I., Lotti, F., Pavan, N., Richenberg, J., ..., & Rocher, L. (2026). ESR Essentials: MRI of the scrotum-practice recommendations by the European Society of Urogenital Radiology. European radiology.
title: ESR Essentials: MRI of the scrotum-practice recommendations by the European Society of Urogenital Radiology
abstract: While conventional ultrasonography (US) remains the first-line imaging modality for scrotal pathology, multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) has emerged as a valuable problem-solving tool for indeterminate US findings. Owing to its superior soft-tissue contrast, functional imaging capabilities, and operator independence, mpMRI allows for the precise localization and characterization of scrotal lesions. This paper from the European Society of Urogenital Radiology Scrotal and Penile Imaging Working Group provides a comprehensive, evidence-based overview of scrotal mpMRI for a general radiologist. It details optimized imaging protocols, recommending a standard sequence of T1-weighted, T2-weighted, diffusion-weighted, and subtracted dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging. The article highlights key clinical indications, including the characterization of intratesticular and paratesticular masses, local staging of testicular germ cell tumors, and differentiation between germ cell and sex cord-stromal neoplasms. This paper familiarizes radiologists with normal MRI appearances and MRI findings of common scrotal diseases. Evidence-based recommendations for reporting basic MRI examinations of the scrotum are also provided. The potential of advanced techniques, such as diffusion tensor imaging and proton MR spectroscopy, and the future integration of artificial intelligence and radiomics, are also discussed. We hope the implementation of these recommendations into radiological practice will enhance diagnostic confidence and promote standardized practice in scrotal MRI for radiologists. KEY POINTS: While conventional ultrasound is the first-line modality for scrotal pathology, it can yield inconclusive findings regarding complex mass characterization and local tumor staging. Multiparametric MRI combines anatomical and functional data to accurately characterize scrotal masses, localize impalpable, undescended testes, and provide precise local tumor staging. Scrotal multiparametric MRI serves as a valuable problem-solving tool that enhances diagnostic confidence in sonographically indeterminate cases, prevents unnecessary radical orchiectomies, supports testis-sparing surgery or active surveillance, and standardizes radiological reporting templates to optimize personalized patient management.

citation: Klimovskij, M., Fortunato, R., Florance, C., Blazyte, G., Cepeniene, A., Zilinskas, J., ..., & Dulskas, A. (2026). Predicting LARS with POLARS: Results of a multicentre study. Colorectal disease : the official journal of the Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland, 28(11), e70659.
title: Predicting LARS with POLARS: Results of a multicentre study
journal: Colorectal disease : the official journal of the Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland
abstract: Background Rectum-preserving colorectal surgery, with low or ultra-low anastomosis, became the standard of care with advances in laparoscopic and now robotic surgery. As a downside, it is not uncommon for function to be affected, causing low anterior resection syndrome (LARS), which is a common postoperative challenge. Aim To determine the correlation of using the predictive preoperative POLARS scores with actual postoperative LARS scores for patients undergoing rectal resections with low pelvic anastomosis. Methods A multicentre, prospective study evaluating LARS was conducted with patients undergoing rectal resection with restoration of bowel continuity. Defaecatory function was assessed preoperatively using the POLARS scoring questionnaire and 6 months after the surgery using the LARS scoring questionnaire. The scores were then compared to determine any correlations. Results A total of 310 patients from 13 centres were enrolled, of whom 95 had complete paired POLARS and postoperative LARS score data. POLARS predicted minor LARS in 69 patients (72.6%), whereas 25 patients (26.3%) reported minor LARS postoperatively. Major LARS was predicted by POLARS in 21 patients (22.1%), whereas 24 patients (25.3%) self-reported major LARS postoperatively. Only 7 of these 24 major-LARS cases (29.2%) were correctly categorized as major LARS by POLARS. For detecting major LARS, POLARS showed sensitivity of 29.2%, specificity of 80.3%, positive predictive value of 33.3% and negative predictive value of 77.0%. Spearman correlation between predicted and observed scores was weak but statistically significant (rho = 0.21, p = 0.042). Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated a mean bias of +7.99 points with 95% limits of agreement from -19.23 to 35.20, reflecting systematic overprediction. Conclusions POLARS showed weak positive correlation with postoperative bowel function and demonstrated low sensitivity but moderate specificity for major LARS. It systematically overestimated LARS severity in many patients. While POLARS may help identify some individuals at elevated risk, it is insufficient as a stand-alone tool for accurate prediction of postoperative LARS severity and should be combined with clinical judgement and patient-reported follow-up.

citation: Penha, R. C. C., Ramaswami, R., Nordwall, J., Phillips, A., Helleberg, M., Ganesan, A., ..., & Lundgren, J. (2026). B-cell markers and cancer risk in people with HIV: an integrative case-control and Mendelian randomization analysis. JNCI cancer spectrum, 10(6), pkag119.
title: B-cell markers and cancer risk in people with HIV: an integrative case-control and Mendelian randomization analysis
abstract: Background Early and continuous antiretroviral therapy (ART) reduces cancer risk in people with HIV (PWH), yet residual risk potentially driven by persistent B-cell activation remains. We used observational and genetic triangulation to evaluate whether baseline B-cell biomarkers are associated with subsequent cancer risk. Methods We conducted (1) a nested case-control study within the INSIGHT trials (158 cases and 313 matched controls) assessing B-cell biomarkers (sCD23, sCD27, sCD30, CXCL13) in PWH and (2) 2-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) to evaluate likely causal relationships between these proteins and 23 cancer types using general-population genome-wide association studies. Median time from study entry to cancer diagnosis was 2.9 years. Results In PWH, CXCL13 was associated with overall cancer risk (highest tertile vs lowest tertile odds ratio [OR] 2.36, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.24 to 4.5), driven by infection-related cancers (N = 82; OR = 4.81, 95% CI = 1.76 to 13.1) and lymphoma (N = 36; OR = 9.92, 95% CI = 1.58 to 62.2). The CXCL13 association remained robust among virally suppressed participants (P = .018). sCD30 was also associated with infection-related cancers (OR = 2.77, 95% CI = 1.09 to 7.03). sCD23 showed a linear association with infection-related cancer (OR per SD = 1.42, 95% CI = 1.01 to 2.00), though tertile-based analyses were nonsignificant. In the general population, MR meta-analyses showed null associations for these biomarkers across 23 cancer types (P > .05). Conclusion Our study links B-cell markers with cancer risk in PWH, identifying CXCL13 as a marker of infection-related cancer risk despite effective ART, highlighting a "residual inflammatory gap" for modern risk stratification. The lack of causal MR signals suggests these proteins are markers of HIV-associated immune activation rather than universal etiological factors for cancer.

citation: Awolalu, O., Hudson, J. J. R., & Rass, U. (2026). Off-target suppression of cell proliferation by commercially available DNA2 inhibitors. DNA repair, 167, 103972.
title: Off-target suppression of cell proliferation by commercially available DNA2 inhibitors
abstract: The disease-associated DNA2 nuclease-helicase is critical for the proper processing of stalled DNA replication forks (RFs). DNA2 inhibition therefore has the potential to cause synthetic lethality in cancer cells in which DNA replication stress and RF stalling are prevalent. Several small molecule biochemical inhibitors of DNA2 have been identified. 4-hydroxy-8-nitroquinoline-3-carboxylic acid, known as DNA2 inhibitor C5, has been widely adopted as a tool compound to test the anti-cancer potential of targeting DNA2 in cellular models, and to study the dependence of molecular processes on DNA2 in cells. Here, we show that C5 treatment does not phenocopy DNA2 loss or inactivation in cells. Independently of DNA2, C5, and its derivative d16, strongly inhibit DNA synthesis in S phase of the cell cycle, revealing off-target anti-proliferative activity. Finally, C5 and d16 are unable to inhibit helicase-dependent single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) accumulations generated by a nuclease-dead version of DNA2. These data show that commonly used compounds fail to effectively inhibit DNA2 in cells and highlight potential caveats in the interpretation of published cellular data obtained with C5 and d16. Moreover, our experimental workflow provides an in cellulo analysis pipeline suitable for identifying biologically active DNA2 inhibitors as a tool for fundamental research and validation of DNA2 as an emerging anti-cancer therapeutic target.

citation: Rubio-Contreras, D., Audibert, S., Fernandez, J., Lambuta, R. A., Pateraki, N., Meaburn, K., ..., & Soutoglou, E. (2026). DNA damage at Lamina-Associated Domains triggers nuclear envelope reorganization and chromatin detachment to prevent nuclear envelope blebbing and genome instability. bioRxiv.
title: DNA damage at Lamina-Associated Domains triggers nuclear envelope reorganization and chromatin detachment to prevent nuclear envelope blebbing and genome instability
abstract: The nuclear periphery anchors large, transcriptionally silent chromatin domains to the nuclear envelope and plays a central role in maintaining genome stability, acting as a dynamic hub for DNA repair. Nevertheless, how cells process DNA damage within lamina-associated domains (LADs), which reside in this environment, remains poorly understood, despite their relevance to nuclear architecture, aging, and senescence. By employing systems for temporally controlled and spatially precise induction of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) within LADs, we show that DSBs within LADs trigger remodeling of the nuclear lamina and the dynamic detachment of damaged LADs from the nuclear envelope, resulting in their relocalization to the nuclear interior. This process is orchestrated by the ATM–γH2AX–MDC1–RNF168–53BP1 axis and requires the linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton (LINC) complex and cytoskeletal components while leaving DNA repair pathway choice unchanged. Persistent tethering of damaged LADs at the nuclear periphery delays the DNA damage response and repair, elevates genomic instability, and drives chromatin extrusion through nuclear blebs directly linking failed repair to dysregulation of nuclear integrity. These findings reveal a protective mechanism in which ATM-driven LAD dynamics and nuclear envelope remodeling might relieve mechanical stress, facilitate repair, and safeguard both genome stability and nuclear architecture.

citation: Zinovkin, D. A., Korneva, Y. S., Arafat, H. M., Shamallakh, O. M., Zinovkina, E. S., Davydov, D. A., Portyanko, A. S., Slepokurova, I. I., Lyzikova, Y. A., & Pranjol, M. Z. I. (2026). Cancer-associated fibroblasts and innate immune cells: orchestrators of the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Frontiers in immunology, 17, 1876751.
title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts and innate immune cells: orchestrators of the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment
abstract: The tumor microenvironment (TME) represents a complex, dynamic, and heterogeneous system in which stromal and immune elements interact to influence tumor development and mechanisms of immune escape. Within the stromal compartment, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) have been identified as key mediators of immune regulation in the TME. Emerging evidence indicates that CAFs engage in extensive crosstalk with innate immune cell populations-including myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs), natural killer (NK) cells, mast cells, and dendritic cells (DCs). Through these interactions, CAFs contribute to the establishment and maintenance of an immunosuppressive milieu that supports tumor progression and facilitates immune evasion. This review summarizes the molecular interactions between CAFs and innate immune cells in the TME. It highlights how CAF-derived factors such as IL-6, TGF-β, CXCL12, and CSF-1 regulate immune cell recruitment and polarization, promoting immunosuppression, tumor progression, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Additionally, feedback signals from immune cells further sustain CAF activation, creating a self-reinforcing immunosuppressive microenvironment. Elucidating these multidirectional interactions offers important insights into tumor biology and identifies promising therapeutic avenues. Targeting CAF-associated signaling pathways or interfering with CAF-immune cell communication may help restore anti-tumor immune responses and improve the effectiveness of cancer immunotherapy strategies.

citation: Capatina, A. L., Malcolm, J. R., Ahmed, A., Bruce, J., Buchanan, P. J., Eykyn, T. R., ..., & Brackenbury, W. J. (2026). Harnessing the ion transportome to treat cancer. The Journal of physiology, 604(22), 8879-8899.
title: Harnessing the ion transportome to treat cancer
abstract: Despite significant advances in early detection and therapeutic opportunities, cancer remains a critical global health challenge. The greatest barrier to reducing cancer-associated mortality is the persistent problem of therapeutic resistance and metastasis. Standard treatment approaches, including surgery combined with chemotherapy and radiation, are effective for many patients with localised disease. However, a substantial proportion of patients will experience recurrence and therapy resistance, leading to treatment failure and poor outcomes. This adverse prognosis for patients highlights the critical need to identify new therapeutic targets capable of improving long-term survival. The ion transportome comprises ion channels, solute transporters and pumps that regulate controlled movement of sodium (Na + ), potassium (K + ), calcium (Ca 2+ ), chloride (Cl - ) and hydrogen (H + ) across cell membranes. Ion transport is central to many cellular processes, including cell growth, volume regulation, proliferation and migration. In many solid tumours, the finely tuned ionic balance becomes dysregulated, with aberrant expression or activity of membrane transport proteins being closely linked to many of the hallmarks of cancer. Ion channel modulation using pharmacological agents designed to treat channelopathies has demonstrated promise in suppressing cancer progression in preclinical models. Thus, targeting ion-driven vulnerabilities within solid tumours may complement existing therapies to overcome resistance and improve patient outcomes. The dynamic nature of ion transport mechanisms means that addressing critical research questions regarding their suitability as pharmacological targets is challenging, highlighting the need to develop innovative approaches to study these processes in oncology.

citation: Mayar, E. M., & Sim, S. Y. (2026). When Appearances Deceive: A Silent Somatotroph Macroadenoma Presenting With Acromegaloid Features and Paradoxically Low Insulin-Like Growth Factor-1. Cureus, 18(10), e118088.
title: When Appearances Deceive: A Silent Somatotroph Macroadenoma Presenting With Acromegaloid Features and Paradoxically Low Insulin-Like Growth Factor-1
abstract: Silent somatotroph adenomas are uncommon pituitary neuroendocrine tumours (PitNETs) of the PIT1 lineage that express growth hormone (GH) immunohistochemically but without biochemical evidence of acromegaly. We report the case of a 32-year-old male patient referred with recurrent epistaxis, headache, right-sided diplopia, and third cranial nerve palsy. Clinical examination revealed acromegaloid features including frontal bossing, spade-like hands, and coarse facies, which were strongly suggestive of longstanding GH excess. However, preoperative insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) was paradoxically low at 13.1 nmol/L (reference range 15.5-33.1 nmol/L), creating a striking clinical-biochemical discordance. MRI demonstrated a giant sellar and suprasellar mass with chiasmal compression, right cavernous sinus invasion, and extension into the paranasal sinuses. The patient underwent endoscopic transsphenoidal resection. Neuropathology confirmed a densely granulated PIT1-lineage somatotroph adenoma with scattered GH positivity, diffuse Pit-1 staining, and a Ki-67 index below 2%. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge posed by silent somatotroph adenomas, underscores the limitations of biochemical assessment alone, and reinforces the essential role of histopathology and immunohistochemistry in establishing a definitive diagnosis. Long-term endocrine and neurosurgical surveillance is strongly recommended given the potential for phenotypic transformation to a functioning acromegaly syndrome.

citation: Brembilla, G., Messina, E., Barret, T., Caglic, I., Cuocolo, R., de Rooij, M., ..., & ESUR Prostate MRI Working Group (2026). Prostate cancer screening with MRI: insights from the ESUR Prostate MRI Working Group. European radiology.
title: Prostate cancer screening with MRI: insights from the ESUR Prostate MRI Working Group
abstract: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening for prostate cancer (PCa) remains controversial due to uncertain long-term benefits, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment of indolent disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has transformed the diagnostic pathway of PCa and is increasingly explored as a screening tool. This special report from the ESUR Prostate MRI Working Group provides an overview of current evidence and insights into the potential role of MRI in PCa screening. MRI-based screening strategies appear to improve detection of clinically significant PCa while reducing unnecessary biopsies and diagnoses of non-significant disease, though long-term outcome data, including mortality impact and interval cancer rates, remain limited. Biparametric MRI is particularly suited for screening due to its shorter acquisition time, reduced operational complexity, and lower costs compared with multiparametric MRI. Two main implementation approaches have emerged: MRI-first pathways, which maximise detection but require substantial resources, and risk-stratified strategies, in which MRI is used after initial assessment (e.g. PSA), potentially offering greater feasibility and cost-effectiveness. Evidence from large trials supports integrating MRI into screening pathways, particularly as a reflex test after PSA screening, although uncertainties remain regarding optimal protocols, interpretation thresholds, follow-up strategies, and long-term outcomes. Key barriers include limited MRI capacity, economic considerations, and the need for standardisation and quality assurance. Advances in artificial intelligence may further enhance efficiency. Overall, MRI has the potential to improve the balance between benefits and harms in PCa screening, but further evidence is required to define its optimal implementation. KEY POINTS: Question Can prostate MRI be effectively integrated into population-based prostate cancer screening pathways? Findings MRI-based screening improves detection of csPCa while reducing unnecessary biopsies; biparametric MRI should be the protocol of choice to enhance feasibility, although optimal implementation and long-term outcomes remain uncertain. Clinical relevance MRI may overcome key limitations of PSA-based screening by enhancing the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer while reducing harms such as overdiagnosis and unnecessary biopsies.

citation: Elsewafy, M., Knox, N., Punchihewa, C., Amro, S., Lankester, K., Kaushik, S., Singh, N., & Dizdarevic, S. (2026). The impact and value of [18F]-FDG PET-CT on management of patients with cervical cancer with service evaluation audited against national evidence-based PET-CT guidelines. Nuclear medicine communications.
title: The impact and value of [18F]-FDG PET-CT on management of patients with cervical cancer with service evaluation audited against national evidence-based PET-CT guidelines
abstract: Purpose First, to assess the diagnostic value of fluorine-18-fluorodeoxyglucose PET-computed tomography ([18F]-FDG PET-CT) compared with conventional MRI and/or CT. Second, to audit the clinical indications for referring patients with cervical cancer for [18F]-FDG PET-CT against the 2022 guidelines published by the Royal College of Radiologists and the Royal College of Physicians. Finally, to evaluate the impact of [18F]-FDG PET-CT on management plans. Methods A retrospective cohort study of 49 patients with histologically proven cervical cancer across the Sussex Cancer Network underwent 59 [18F]-FDG PET-CT between 1 November 2020 and 31 October 2022. Scans were compared with the most recent CT and MRI scan conducted within 4 months of the [18F]-FDG PET-CT. Scan indications were categorized as either 'in accordance' or 'outside' the guidelines. Those in accordance fell into one of four groups: staging, response assessment, suspected recurrence, or staging when considering exenterative surgery. A questionnaire investigating the impact of the [18F]-FDG PET-CT on the management plan of each patient was answered by one clinical oncology consultant. Results [18F]-FDG PET-CT identified new metastatic sites in 16/59 (27.1%) scans. The remaining scans were concordant with the CT and MRI. The majority, 57/59 (96.6%), of the scans were performed in accordance with the guidelines. The management plan was changed by 5/59 scans (8.4%), confirmed by 48/59 (81.4%) and was not impacted with 6/59 (10.2%) scans. Conclusion [18F]-FDG PET-CT is superior to conventional imaging and enhances the management plan. Future cohort studies with larger patient numbers involving multicentric studies are needed to fully assess its impact on cervical cancer management and prognosis.

citation: Palmer, D. A., Ogilvie-Park, D., Muir, A. L., Craig, R., Sevim, O., Stott, L., ..., & Morgan, R. G. (2026). RUNX1 aberrations in blast-phase chronic myeloid leukaemia induce the RNA-binding protein SPATS2L, which promotes growth, survival and stress granule assembly. Leukemia.
title: RUNX1 aberrations in blast-phase chronic myeloid leukaemia induce the RNA-binding protein SPATS2L, which promotes growth, survival and stress granule assembly
abstract: RUNX1 is a critical regulator of hematopoiesis. In CML, somatic RUNX1 mutations and RUNX1::MECOM/EVI1, are associated with TKI resistance and progression to BP-CML. To examine post-transcriptional dysregulation downstream of RUNX1 aberrations, we used orthogonal organic phase separation to characterise the RNA-binding proteome of RUNX1 deficient BP-CML cells. RUNX1 depleted BP-CML cells exhibited significant alterations to RBPs involved in stress response pathways and translation/ribosome-biogenesis. Furthermore, RUNX1 depletion or expression of RUNX1::EVI1 in BP-CML cells induced expression and RNA binding activity of SPATS2L, a component of stress granules (SG). Whilst RUNX1 depletion increased SG-assembly, SPATS2L depletion reduced SG-assembly and inhibited the growth/survival of multiple BP-CML cell lines. Homoharringtonine (HHT), used historically in TKI-resistant CML, ablated SG-assembly in BP-CML cells with RUNX1 depletion, and primary BP-CML cells with LOF/hypomorphic RUNX1 mutations were preferentially sensitised to HHT. Suppressing SPATS2L expression induced by RUNX1 depletion, reduced SG-forming capacity and increased the HHT-sensitivity of RUNX1 depleted BP-CML cells, suggesting SPATS2L contributes to therapeutic resistance in RUNX1 mutated CML. Finally, we demonstrate that SGs may contribute more widely to TKI-resistance in this setting. This study suggests that SPATS2L/SG induction could be critical to RUNX1-mutant leukemias, and, provides preliminary evidence for a mutationally-targeted approach in CML with RUNX1 aberrations.

citation: Mayar, E. M., Crown, A., & Sim, S. Y. (2026). From Trauma to Tumour: Incidental Giant Left Adrenal Myelolipoma in Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia. Cureus, 18(10), e117583.
title: From Trauma to Tumour: Incidental Giant Left Adrenal Myelolipoma in Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia
abstract: Adrenal myelolipomas are rare, benign tumours composed of mature adipose and haematopoietic tissue. Patients with congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) are predisposed to their development, with chronic adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) hypersecretion secondary to impaired cortisol synthesis thought to be the principal driver of myelolipoma formation in this population. A 49-year-old female with known CAH presented to the emergency department following a stab wound to the abdomen. Computed tomography (CT) incidentally identified a 12 cm encapsulated left adrenal lesion consistent with a giant myelolipoma. Despite reported adherence to hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement therapy, persistently elevated adrenal steroid precursors and plasma renin levels suggested suboptimal glucocorticoid control. Following multidisciplinary team (MDT) review, the patient was offered a left adrenalectomy given the lesion size (>10 cm) and concerns regarding the risk of spontaneous haemorrhage. This case underscores the importance of systematic imaging review beyond the primary indication for scanning, and the value of optimising biochemical monitoring and considering adrenal imaging in selected high-risk CAH patients.

citation: Grice, S., Gardner, J., Thomson, P., Hering, L., MacDonald, L., Collins, S., ..., & Naisbitt, D. J. (2026). Immune checkpoint inhibition enhances memory T-cell responses to CEF(T), SARS-CoV-2 spike proteins and ChAdOx1 nCoV-19. Human vaccines & immunotherapeutics, 22(1), 2742035.
title: Immune checkpoint inhibition enhances memory T-cell responses to CEF(T), SARS-CoV-2 spike proteins and ChAdOx1 nCoV-19
abstract: An extensive body of clinical and experimental evidence demonstrates that immune checkpoint blockade can invigorate recall immune responses. This phenomenon has previously been highlighted using ex vivo (healthy donor) and in vivo (immunotherapy patients) models of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) administration that demonstrate an enhancement of the T-cell response to concomitant small-molecule drugs. However, the immunological and clinical impact of ICI therapy pre-ceding vaccination, where robust antigen-specific immunogenicity is essential, remains poorly defined. In this study, we utilized an ex vivo assay to evaluate lymphocyte recall responses within peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) derived from healthy donors and patients pre- and post-immunotherapy following exposure to SARS-CoV-2 derived peptides and ChAdOx1 nCoV-19. In line with the anticipated effects of the primary pharmacology of immune checkpoint inhibitors, we outline an acute increase in proliferation and cytokine and cytolytic molecule secretion following immune checkpoint blockade in response to CEF(T), wild-type SARS-CoV-2 spike pools 1 and 2, and ChAdOx1 nCoV-19. Future studies are needed to evaluate the clinical correlates of the veracity of such responses with protection and incidence of adverse events.

citation: El-Taji, O., Dutey-Magni, P., Brown, M., Murray, M., Amos, C., Gilbert, D., ..., & STAMPEDE Collaborators (2026). Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events in Men with High-risk Localized or Metastatic Prostate Cancer Starting Long-term Hormone Therapy in the STAMPEDE Trial. European urology, S0302-2838(26)02370-5.
title: Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events in Men with High-risk Localized or Metastatic Prostate Cancer Starting Long-term Hormone Therapy in the STAMPEDE Trial
abstract: Background Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) are a leading cause of noncancer death in men with prostate cancer (PCa). Androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs) improve oncologic outcomes but may exacerbate cardiovascular risk. The Systematic Coronary Risk Evaluation 2(SCORE2) estimates 10-yr cardiovascular risk, yet its validity in men receiving treatment for PCa is untested. Objective To evaluate the cardiovascular safety of ARPIs and other treatment intensification strategies within the STAMPEDE trial and assess SCORE2 performance. Design, setting, and participants This post hoc analysis included patients allocated to the abiraterone acetate plus prednisolone (AAP), AAP plus enzalutamide (ENZ), docetaxel (DOC), zoledronic acid (ZA), and radiotherapy (RT) comparisons in STAMPEDE with linked health care records in England. Intervention Treatment intensification with AAP, AAP plus ENZ, DOC, ZA, or prostate RT in addition to standard-of-care androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). Outcome measurements and statistical analysis MACE were identified using prespecified International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, and Office of Population Censuses and Surveys Classification of Interventions and Procedures codes. Flexible parametric competing-risk models estimated cumulative incidence and subdistribution hazard ratios (SDHRs). SCORE2 discrimination and calibration were evaluated. Results and limitations A total of 6292 men were included. The 5-yr cumulative MACE incidence with ARPI intensification was 9% in nonmetastatic (M0) disease and 7% in metastatic (M1) disease, comparable to ADT alone. ARPI intensification was not associated with a statistically significant increase in MACE risk (AAP: M0 SDHR 1.15 [95% confidence interval {CI} 0.80-1.67], M1 SDHR 1.36 [95% CI 0.87-2.10]; AAP plus ENZ: M0 SDHR 1.34 [95% CI 0.91-1.98], M1 SDHR 1.28 [95% CI 0.85-1.94]). Cardiovascular disease history was the strongest predictor of MACE. Among 5076 patients eligible for SCORE2 assessment, 4239 had complete baseline data. SCORE2 discrimination was modest (10-yr area under the curve 0.63 for M0 disease and 0.61 for M1 disease), and absolute cardiovascular risk was underestimated. Limitations included underrepresentation of patients with severe cardiovascular comorbidity. Conclusions No statistically significant increase in MACE was observed with ARPIs, DOC, ZA, or prostate RT compared with ADT alone. SCORE2 underestimated cardiovascular risk, supporting development of PCa-specific cardiovascular risk models.

citation: Kennedy, E., Stott, L., Ashworth, I., Ladikou, E., Jones, J. R., Johnston, R., ..., & Pepper, A. G. (2026). TLR9-dependent migration identifies different Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia signaling states under BTK inhibition. Blood, blood.2025032914.
title: TLR9-dependent migration identifies different Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia signaling states under BTK inhibition
abstract: B-cell receptor (BCR) inhibitors have transformed chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) therapy, yet many patients show incomplete responses or develop resistance in the absence of Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) mutations. We investigated Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) signaling as a tumor-response mechanism to BCR blockade. Using 102 TLR9-stimulated patient samples, we identified two distinct migratory phenotypes: TLR9-induced migratory Responders (R), with enhanced migration, and TLR9-induced migratory Reverse-Responders (RR), with suppression of migration following TLR9 activation. Transcriptomic and protein analyses showed TLR9-stimulated R samples expressed higher IRAK4/IRAK1 and induced NF-kB p100, consistent with intact TLR9 signaling. In contrast, RR samples exhibited elevated basal BCR activity, and lower IRAK4/IRAK1 with rapid IRAK1 degradation, indicating suppressed TLR9 signaling. In-silico modeling and biochemical validation showed high basal BCR signaling suppresses TLR9 responsiveness, whereas low basal activity permits full TLR9 activation. Functionally, TLR9-induced migration persisted despite BTK inhibition (BTKi) in R but not RR samples, and was abrogated by TLR9 antagonism, consistent with signaling through a BTK-independent pathway in the R subgroup. CLL cells from BTKi-resistant patients expressed higher TLR9 and matched pre- and post-relapse samples showed decreased BCR and increased TLR-associated NF-kB signaling post-relapse. Clinically, in small exploratory.

citation: Ouyang, C., Sun, K., Wang, F., Ye, F., Zhu, L., Dong, L., ..., & Guo, Z. (2026). Microsatellite expansion redirects chromatin modifiers to confer insect resistance to Bt bioinsecticides. Nucleic acids research, 54(20), gkag1058.
title: Microsatellite expansion redirects chromatin modifiers to confer insect resistance to Bt bioinsecticides
abstract: Microsatellites are highly mutable genomic elements, yet their role in adaptive gene regulation in insects remains poorly understood. Here, we show that a tetranucleotide (ATGT) microsatellite expansion in the promoter of ABCC2, a key Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) toxin receptor gene, epigenetically silences its expression and confers resistance to Bt Cry1Ac toxin in Plutella xylostella (L.). Mechanistically, long repeats (≥27 units) in Cry1Ac-resistant strains preferentially recruit the histone methyltransferase E(z), promoting H3K27me2/3 deposition, chromatin compaction, and transcriptional silencing, whereas short repeats in susceptible strains maintain open chromatin through Tip60-mediated H4K5 acetylation. This repeat expansion alone is sufficient to repress ABCC2, thereby conferring Bt resistance, while repeat length, chromatin state, and associated phenotypes partially revert under relaxed selection. These findings define a previously uncharacterized cis-acting element dynamically orchestrating insecticide resistance-associated gene expression and identify microsatellite-driven chromatin remodeling as a general and plastic regulatory strategy underlying rapid xenobiotic-resistance evolution in insects.

citation: Al-Hussain, S. A., Alharbi, A. S., Muhammad, Z. A., Halim, A. S. A., Zaki, M. E. A., Bagley, M. C., & Kassab, R. M. (2026). Diethylene Glycol-Linked Ring-Fused Bis-Azoles: Target-Oriented Synthesis, In Silico Screening, and Antitumor Activity. ChemMedChem, 21(19), e70504.
title: Diethylene Glycol-Linked Ring-Fused Bis-Azoles: Target-Oriented Synthesis, In Silico Screening, and Antitumor Activity
abstract: The target-oriented synthesis of diethylene glycol-linked bis-imidazo- and bis-thiazolo ring-fused mono-, bi-, and tricyclic derivatives was accomplished using inexpensive reagents, bis-phenacyl bromide derivative 4, and thiosemicarbazone 6. The diethylene glycol-linked architectures included bis(thiazolo[3,2-a]pyrimidinone) derivatives 8a,b, bis(imidazo-azole) derivatives 12-14, bis(imidazo-thiazole) derivatives 17,18, and bis-thiazoles 20a-g. Cytotoxic evaluation against liver, lung, colon, and prostate human tumor cell lines found remarkable selectivity to hepatocellular carcinoma (HepG2) cells. The most potent bis-imidazo- and bis-thiazolo-fused derivatives 8a,b, 12 and 13 demonstrated cytotoxicity against HepG2 cells (IC 50 6.8-17.8 µM) with exceptional selectivity (SI 5.6-14.6) compared with cisplatin (SI 2.4). Further screening of their VEGFR-2 TK and FGFR-2 TK inhibition showed that 8a had moderate activity, whereas phenyl-substituted derivative 8b displayed promising anti-VEGFR-2 and remarkable anti-FGFR-2 activities, with IC 50 0.19 ± 0.01 and 0.03 ± 0.01 µM, respectively, compared with the reference drugs sorafenib (IC 50 0.12 ± 0.01) and staurosporine (IC 50 0.03 ± 0.01 µM). The inhibition of VEGFR-2 and FGFR-2 TKs was supported by molecular docking studies, with compound 8b showing binding affinity to the VEGFR-2 and FGFR-2 ATP binding pockets. Pharmacokinetics and ADMET drug-likeness evaluation indicated that bis(thiazolo[3,2-a]pyrimidinone) derivatives 8a and 8b have drug-like properties.

citation: Jayachandran, A., Mütze, M., Romaniuk, K., Hudson, J. J. R., Dello Stritto, M. R., Guérois, R., ..., & Cejka, P. (2026). Human PIF1 clears secondary DNA structures by coupled DNA unwinding and rewinding activities. Genes & development, 40(19-20), 1747-1764.
title: Human PIF1 clears secondary DNA structures by coupled DNA unwinding and rewinding activities
abstract: PIF1 family helicases promote genome stability during DNA replication and repair, yet the biochemical activity of human PIF1 (hPIF1) remains poorly understood. Here, we directly compare full-length hPIF1 and budding yeast Pif1 (yPif1) and show that the two enzymes operate differently. In bulk assays, hPIF1 displays weak net DNA unwinding because its robust intrinsic single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) annealing activity rapidly reforms duplex DNA behind the helicase motor. Single-molecule magnetic tweezers experiments reveal that hPIF1 is only modestly slower than yPif1 and similarly processive, indicating that poor apparent unwinding primarily reflects rapid reannealing rather than impaired motor activity. Mutagenesis and structural modeling indicate that this functional divergence depends on a yeast-specific insertion within the catalytic domain. Unlike yPif1, hPIF1 fails to stimulate Polδ-dependent displacement-loop (D-loop) extension, arguing that it does not promote DNA unwinding ahead of the migrating bubble. However, similarly to yPif1, hPIF1 likely unwinds newly synthesized DNA coupled with DNA reannealing behind the migrating D-loop. hPIF1 efficiently remodels intramolecular G-quadruplex DNA into fully base-paired dsDNA, whereas yPif1 generates ssDNA products. Together, our data support a model in which hPIF1 acts primarily as a DNA translocase that couples local unwinding with rapid rewinding to clear secondary DNA structures without generating extensive ssDNA.

citation: Ling, R. E., Welsh, A. M. N., Hamer, L., Jackson, T., Neil, E., Elliott, N., ..., & Roy, A. (2026). LIN28B is essential for human fetal B-lymphopoiesis and initiation of KMT2A::AFF1 infant leukemia. Blood, 148(17), 2146-2158.
title: LIN28B is essential for human fetal B-lymphopoiesis and initiation of KMT2A::AFF1 infant leukemia
abstract: Abstract Infant acute lymphoblastic leukemia (iALL) is initiated in utero, most often by rearrangements of the KMT2A gene (KMT2Ar). It carries a very poor prognosis despite a lack of additional oncogenic driver mutations common in childhood ALL. Here, we aimed to identify specific properties of human fetal hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPC) that promote leukemic transformation in KMT2Ar iALL using molecular, functional, and in vivo assays. Through comparison of human fetal HSPC with adult HSPC transcriptomes we derived a fetal development-specific gene signature and identified the fetal oncogene LIN28B and its downstream effectors among the top hits. These genes were also expressed in iALL. Functional assays revealed that LIN28B was essential in normal human fetal liver (FL) CD34+ cells to maintain proliferation and stem-like properties, and support B-cell and natural killer cell lymphopoiesis. To interrogate the role of LIN28B in iALL, we used a human FL-derived CRISPR-CRISPR-associated protein 9 KMT2A::AFF1 model. In this CRISPRKMT2A::AFF1 model, human FL CD34+ cells fail to transform upon induction of KMT2A::AFF1 translocation in the absence of LIN28B. Furthermore, LIN28B-expressing CRISPRKMT2A::AFF1 leukemias were more proliferative in vitro and in vivo, with this advantage being lost upon LIN28B knockdown. Mechanistic studies showed that LIN28B acts by stabilizing key early B-lymphoid genes, epigenetic regulators, and cell cycle and antiapoptotic genes. Thus, LIN28B has an essential role in normal human fetal B-lymphopoiesis and is necessary for initiation of KMT2A::AFF1 iALL in human fetal cells in the absence of cooperating mutations. LIN28B activity contributes to the aggressive behavior of KMT2A::AFF1 ALL, making it an attractive target in LIN28B-expressing leukemias.

citation: Flauto, F., Neola, G., Cimadamore, A., Maffezzoli, M., Maniam, A., Scagliarini, S., Calabrò, F., Formisano, L., Rescigno, P., & Banna, G. L. (2026). Non-conventional histologies of prostate cancer: from morphology to biology-driven precision oncology. The oncologist, 31(11), oyag391.
title: Non-conventional histologies of prostate cancer: from morphology to biology-driven precision oncology
abstract: Non-conventional prostate cancer histologies represent a small but clinically significant subset characterized by aggressive behavior, atypical biomarker profiles, and reduced dependence on androgen receptor signaling. Evidence indicates these histologies reflect dynamic biological states driven by genomic instability, lineage plasticity, and therapeutic selection rather than static morphologic entities, with several morphologies acting as accessible, if imperfect, surrogates for actionable alterations. We performed a translational narrative review integrating anatomic pathology, genomic and epigenomic biology, and biomarker-selected therapy, searching PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, the ASCO Meeting Library, ESMO publications, and APCCC through May 2026, spanning neuroendocrine, ductal, intraductal, cribriform, adenosquamous, sarcomatoid, adenoid cystic, signet ring cell, and mucinous subtypes. These histologies are individually uncommon but are consistently associated with advanced stage and inferior survival. Neuroendocrine prostate cancer is the most aggressive phenotype and a major mechanism of resistance to AR-directed therapy, driven by combined RB1 and TP53 loss, epigenetic reprogramming, and lineage plasticity, and marked by DLL3 expression. Cribriform and intraductal carcinoma are often enriched for BRCA2 and DNA-repair deficiency, whereas ductal differentiation is associated with mismatch-repair deficiency in a subset, with implications for PARP inhibition and checkpoint blockade. Emerging strategies include platinum-based chemoimmunotherapy and investigational lineage-directed agents targeting DLL3, STEAP1, KLK2, and TROP-2, alongside radioligands. These histologies are best viewed as biologically distinct, evolving disease states. By integrating pathology, molecular biology, and biomarker-selected therapy into one translational pathway, this review reframes non-conventional histology as a prompt for early molecular characterization and adaptive, biology-driven treatment.

citation: Martin-Guerrero, S. M., Shields, T., Casado, P., Zach, R., Rajeeve, V., Afroz-Nishat, N., ..., & Cutillas, P. R. (2026). Greatwall kinase regulates acute myeloid leukaemia cell division through a non-canonical mechanism. EMBO reports, 27(21), 6464-6488.
title: Greatwall kinase regulates acute myeloid leukaemia cell division through a non-canonical mechanism
abstract: Greatwall kinase regulates mitotic progression by phosphorylating ENSA and ARPP19, thereby inhibiting PP2A-B55. Moreover, Greatwall has been implicated in oncogenesis, particularly in solid tumours, but the mechanisms by which Greatwall regulates the cell cycle in other malignancies remain unclear. Here, we show that Greatwall regulates cytokinesis and cell cycle progression in acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) cells through a pathway distinct from ENSA-PP2A-B55. AML cells require Greatwall expression and activity to proliferate, as revealed by pharmacological and systematic genetic perturbation experiments. Mechanistically, Greatwall inactivation or genetic depletion does not measurably affect the ENSA-PP2A-B55 pathway. Instead, loss of Greatwall function alters cytokinesis, and the phosphorylation of proteins involved in cytoskeletal organisation and cytokinesis, including MARK3, which we identify as a direct Greatwall substrate in AML cells. Together, these findings reveal that the Greatwall kinase signalling network is wired differently in leukemic cells, thus uncovering a novel mechanism of cell cycle regulation.

citation: Leta, G. T., Tasew, G., Getachew, B., Henry, C., Abera, A., Mengiste, T. B., ..., & Gebretsadik, F. S. (2026). Burden of schistosomiasis in Ethiopia following 10 years of preventive chemotherapy: a national cross-sectional geostatistical survey. The Lancet. Global health, 14(11), 104037.
title: Burden of schistosomiasis in Ethiopia following 10 years of preventive chemotherapy: a national cross-sectional geostatistical survey
abstract: Background Current strategies aim to eliminate schistosomiasis as a public health problem globally by 2030. As this target approaches, up-to-date knowledge of the burden and distribution of schistosomiasis is crucial. After a decade of control measures in Ethiopia, there are currently no high-resolution data with which to evaluate progress and guide interventions. Through a nationwide survey, we aimed to map the fine-scale distribution of schistosomiasis in Ethiopia to guide programmatic decision making at the kebele (subdistrict) level. Methods This cross-sectional geostatistical survey was conducted across ten regions of Ethiopia using spatially regulated sampling. Children aged 9-14 years were selected, using sex-stratified systematic random sampling, from schools or communities. Stool samples, collected from children in all ten regions, were assessed for Schistosoma mansoni using the Kato-Katz thick smear technique. Schistosoma haematobium infection was assessed by urine filtration and a urine dipstick test from samples obtained from children in three endemic regions. We fitted geostatistical models incorporating environmental covariates from five domains: sociodemographic, bioclimate, geology, land cover, and exposure to contaminated water. We generated 1 km 2 prevalence maps and estimated the probability of exceeding WHO preventive chemotherapy thresholds at the kebele level. The primary outcomes were the prevalences of infection and heavy-intensity infection with S mansoni and S haematobium. Findings Between June 20, 2021, and Oct 22, 2024, 121 593 children were enrolled at 4258 sites. Complete datasets for S mansoni analysis were available from 119 559 children surveyed at 4100 sites, among whom 26 885 were also assessed for S haematobium. The mean age of the children was 11·4 years (SD 1·7), with 57 046 (47·7%) female and 62 513 (52·3%) male. The combined survey prevalence of both Schistosoma species analysed was 5·4% (95% CI 5·0-5·9): 5·2% (4·8-5·7) for S mansoni and 1·0% (0·8-1·3) for S haematobium. Compared with baseline defined woreda-level prevalence categories, areas with a prevalence of at least 10% have declined, reducing the number of people above the threshold for requiring annual preventive chemotherapy from 25·6 million to 10·8 million. 1622 (11·0%) of 14 763 assessed kebeles were above the threshold for annual preventive chemotherapy, and the predicted probability of correct classification was at least 70% for 11 600 (78·6%) of the 14 763 kebeles. The prevalence of heavy-intensity infection among the survey population was 0·2% (95% CI 0·2 to 0·3) overall (0·2% [0·2 to 0·3] for S mansoni and Interpretation This national, high-resolution map of schistosomiasis in Ethiopia shows marked progress towards elimination. The model-based geostatistical approach supports targeted, evidence-driven interventions and more efficient use of resources. Funding END Fund's Deworming Innovation Fund, which receives funding from anchor partners including the ELMA Foundation, Delta Philanthropies, the Children's Investment Fund Foundation, the Wyss Medical Foundation, and Virgin Unite through an Audacious Project.

citation: Bakr, L., Bakr, S., Chaubey, M., Binti Mohd Azhari, H., Peryt, A., Coonar, A. S., & Aresu, G. (2026). Training the next generation in uniportal video-assisted thoracic surgery: A single-centre retrospective cohort study of operative and oncological outcomes. Surgical oncology, 69, 102575.
title: Training the next generation in uniportal video-assisted thoracic surgery: A single-centre retrospective cohort study of operative and oncological outcomes
abstract: Background Uniportal video-assisted thoracic surgery presents distinct technical demands that challenge traditional assumptions about surgical training. Evidence remains limited on how trainees are introduced to the technique in clinical practice and what outcomes follow. Methods A retrospective cohort study at Royal Papworth Hospital, including all uniportal VATS anatomical lung resections and thymectomies performed between May 2023 and August 2024; thymectomies were analysed separately. Cases were categorised as training, where the trainee was recorded as primary operator under consultant supervision, or non-training. The two groups differ as consultants assigned cases at their discretion according to perceived complexity. Mortality was followed to 8 August 2026. Post-operative morbidity was classified using the Clavien-Dindo system. Continuous differences are reported as Hodges-Lehmann location shifts with bootstrap confidence intervals. Operative time was modelled on the log scale, with confidence intervals bootstrapped over operators, and all comparisons were repeated excluding the highest-volume registrar. Results Out of 203 anatomical lung resections in 202 patients, 100 were training and 103 non-training. Measured baseline characteristics were similar, although the two groups differed in operative complexity. Operative time was longer in the training group but did not reach statistical significance (training median 2.32 versus 2.08 h; Hodges-Lehmann shift +0.20 h, 95% CI -0.08 to +0.52; p = 0.054). Adjusted for procedure type and supervising consultant, training cases were 7.4% longer (95% CI -1.0 to +16.6; p = 0.087); with confidence intervals bootstrapped over operators this widened to -3.6% to +22.5%. Post-operative length of stay was identical, with a median of 3 days in both groups (p = 0.872). There was one death within 30 days, in the non-training group, and one further death within 90 days, in the training group; these numbers are too small to support any comparison.
